newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chips drop on Fed rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chips drop on Fed rate fears.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell in early trading Tuesday as investors turned cautious, mulling the possibility that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates for the second time in as many months.
Shortly before 11 a.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 66.76 points at 7,162.12.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances by a 3-1 margin on light volume of 102 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the central bank's policy-making arm, began meeting at 9 a.m. EDT 1300 GMT and was expected to announce a decision on interest rates around 2:15 p.m. EDT 1815 GMT.

At its last meeting in March, the inflation-wary Fed raised the key federal funds rate -- the rate commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans -- by one quarter percentage point. It was the first increase in more than two years.

Recent data has shown that inflation is not a threat. The Producer Price Index tumbled 0.6 percent in April, its biggest drop in nearly four years, while the Consumer Price Index rose just 0.1 percent.

Economists are split nearly down the middle on the outcome of the Fed's deliberations, with a slight majority forecasting no change in monetary policy, according to a Reuters survey released on Monday.
Arguing for another rate rise: an economy that has been growing too quickly for its own good, a tight jobs market, rising wages and a stock market that may be too exuberant.
Among its options, the central bank could let the federal funds rate stand at 5.5 percent, a decision analysts have said could give the stock market a lift.
Or it could boost rates by another quarter percentage point to make a pre-emptive strike against inflation. That might or might not depress stock markets, analysts said.
A rate rise would mean higher borrowing costs for everyone from consumers using credit cards to the stores where they shop. It also would tend to slow the economy and dampen inflation.
"Investors will stay on the sideline until we know," said Charlie Crane, market strategist at Key Asset Management.

The bond market was also lower, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond off 10/32, which raised its yield to 6.95 percent from 6.92 percent at Monday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The Nasdaq Composite index edged up 0.35 of a point to 1,341.59.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was off 6.70 points at 826.57, and the American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.37 to 587.11.
